input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn corrected three drawing citations, one indefinite part reference and two figure-brief statements, so no claim scope moved. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

Reviewed input/disclosure.md, input/conversation.md (one USER passage; the single YOU passage is context only), input/brief.md (formalities only), draft sections 01–10, draft/numerals.md, and all seven figure briefs. A full ledger was built: every limitation of claims 1–20, every numeral in numerals.md, and every structure, relationship, material, position, connection, result, operating condition and variant in the Summary, Detailed Description and figure briefs was traced to an exact affirmative passage of the disclosure, except for the two items reported below.

Traced and clean: the shell (floor, side walls, upper edge, ledges), the tray (bottom wall, tray side walls, tray feet standing on the floor, perforations, lower return passage, two side supply passages formed by inward spacing), the module (rigid spacer frame, two opposed cassettes confronting across a central space, downward-opening central inlet, two guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, upwardly opening mating channel, resilient feet), the lid (depending indexing rib, compressible gasket sealing after registration, horizontal shift into the registered position, feet pressed against ledges so the module cannot lift away), the complete circulation path, the "free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover" negative, the condensate channel/wick/pull tab/discharge openings, and the full mechanical exposure indicator chain including the latched exposed position, retention after the cassette cools, manual reset only after opening, and non-control of airflow. Claim 12's progressive-engagement limitation traces to "A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration"; claim 5's removability traces to "conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame". The optional-feature designation of the channel, wick, pull tab, discharge openings and indicator traces to "The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features."

Depiction conventions accepted, because the figure briefs tag them "shown schematically" and the claims and description stay shape-neutral: the schematic shell/lid slabs and hatched wall bodies, the rectangular open spacer frame with bottom panel, the flat rectangular cassette slabs drawn as plain closed boxes, the schematic tray feet, the schematic ledge block, the outward step carrying the resilient feet, the wick and pull-tab outlines, and the indicator housing, coil spring and latch block in FIG. 7. Verbalized geometry of functional surfaces was checked separately and each such statement traces to the source: the gasket flattened between lid underside and shell top edge ("compressible ... seals against the upper edge"), the resilient foot flattened between a downwardly facing frame surface and the upwardly facing ledge top ("presses resilient feet ... against ledges"), the rib's lower end received in the upwardly open groove ("the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame"), the outlet opening at the foot of each duct opening sideways into the passage ("descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages"), the duct-foot opening through the downwardly facing bottom surface above the trough ("Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel"), and the shallow trough drawn wider than deep ("shallow condensate channel").

Internal-text checks: numerals 10–100 each denote one part, all are defined in numerals.md and all are used in the description; every figure's numeral list matches both its brief and its Brief Description entry; the "seen in FIG. n" cross-references in the Detailed Description all resolve; the three broken-line curves in FIG. 1 carry the same FIG. 3/FIG. 4/FIG. 5 designations used in the enlargement briefs and in the Brief Description; the section line is designated 7-7 identically in FIG. 6's brief, FIG. 7's brief and both Brief Description entries, with both arrows in one direction that matches FIG. 7's left-facing outer surface and left-projecting stem; FIG. 3/4/5 left-right orientations match their FIG. 1 regions; claims and description use the same relationships and terms; the abstract is a single paragraph under 150 words; cross-reference and government-support statements match input/brief.md (no priority claim, no federal sponsorship); the title matches the working title; and no drafting note, placeholder, open question, instruction, unresolved alternative or internal comment remains.

Three defects require correction before render: one figure-to-figure geometric contradiction in FIG. 5 that would draw the product tray resting at the floor and erase the disclosed lower return passage, and two untraced statements in the Detailed Description (a condensation mechanism imported from the prior-art Background, and a transport result attributing persistence of the registered overlap to the resilient feet). All three fixes are deletions or minimal rewordings; none requires new matter.

## Mechanical checks that did not pass

- **Source fidelity is clean before rendering** (fail): Reviewed input/disclosure.md, input/conversation.md (one USER passage; the single YOU passage is context only), input/brief.md (formalities only), draft sections 01–10, draft/numerals.md, and all seven figure briefs. A full ledger was built: every limitation of claims 1–20, every numeral in numerals.md, and every structure, relationship, material, position, connection, result, operating condition and variant in the Summary, Detailed Description and figure briefs was traced to an exact affirmative passage of the disclosure, except for the two items reported below.

Traced and clean: the shell (floor, side walls, upper edge, ledges), the tray (bottom wall, tray side walls, tray feet standing on the floor, perforations, lower return passage, two side supply passages formed by inward spacing), the module (rigid spacer frame, two opposed cassettes confronting across a central space, downward-opening central inlet, two guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, upwardly opening mating channel, resilient feet), the lid (depending indexing rib, compressible gasket sealing after registration, horizontal shift into the registered position, feet pressed against ledges so the module cannot lift away), the complete circulation path, the "free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover" negative, the condensate channel/wick/pull tab/discharge openings, and the full mechanical exposure indicator chain including the latched exposed position, retention after the cassette cools, manual reset only after opening, and non-control of airflow. Claim 12's progressive-engagement limitation traces to "A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration"; claim 5's removability traces to "conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame". The optional-feature designation of the channel, wick, pull tab, discharge openings and indicator traces to "The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure ind
  - Untraced condensation mechanism: moist ambient air condensing on cassette surfaces and guide-duct walls
  - FIG. 5 brief places the tray bottom wall at the shell floor, erasing the lower return passage and contradicting FIG. 1, FIG. 4 and the description
  - Untraced transport result: the registered outlet-to-passage overlap said to persist through the journey because the resilient feet hold down

## Reviewer findings

- **[critical] Untraced condensation mechanism: moist ambient air condensing on cassette surfaces and guide-duct walls** (draft/08-detailed-description.md, "Condensate management", final sentence of the paragraph at line 35) - The description asserts where and how condensate forms inside the carrier. The disclosure says only that the discharge openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts deliver condensate into the channel; it never states that moist ambient air is admitted whenever the carrier is opened, nor that condensation occurs on the cassette surfaces or on the walls of the guide ducts. No affirmative passage in the disclosure or in the single USER message of the conversation describes the origin or the surfaces of condensation. The only source for this mechanism is the prior-art characterization in draft/05-background.md ("moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space"), and prior art cannot support invention text. This is an untraced operating condition and location assertion, not an inference from a disclosed relationship.
  - Suggested fix: Replace the sentence with the supported statement only: "Condensate present in the guide ducts 50 runs down them and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 into the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods." Delete the clause "Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and". No other section cites this mechanism, so no further edit is needed.
- **[major] FIG. 5 brief places the tray bottom wall at the shell floor, erasing the lower return passage and contradicting FIG. 1, FIG. 4 and the description** (figures/FIG-5.md, paragraph at line 9 ("Below the module body, a thin hatched upright wall ... joined at its lower end b) - FIG. 5 states both that the tray's horizontal bottom wall is joined at the lower end of the thin upright tray wall and that the open vertical space is bounded by that thin wall all the way down to the horizontal bottom body (the floor), with the trough in the top surface of the bottom body at the foot of that space. Taken together this puts the tray's bottom wall at floor level, so no space remains beneath the tray and the perforations described in the same paragraph open into nothing. That contradicts FIG. 1, which holds the tray above the floor on the tray feet with small openings where each gap meets the space beneath the tray; contradicts FIG. 4, where "the open space beneath that bottom wall is the lower return passage 24"; and contradicts the description and claims 1 and 17, which require the tray supported above the floor with a lower return passage between the bottom wall and the floor. Two enlargements of the same section therefore disagree about the height of the tray above the floor.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-5.md, replace that paragraph's first and third sentences with: "Below the module body, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the left of the inner surface of the upright wall body, its lower edge spaced above the top surface of the horizontal bottom body immediately inboard of the trough described below, and a thin hatched horizontal bottom wall joined to that upright wall above its lower edge and extending leftward, the space beneath that bottom wall being open. A series of small openings passes through the product tray where that upright wall meets that bottom wall, as in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. An open vertical space runs down between the upright wall body and the thin wall and continues below the lower edge of the thin wall to the horizontal bottom body, so that the downward opening in the module body stands above that space." Leave the trough, wick and pull-tab sentences unchanged.
- **[major] Untraced transport result: the registered outlet-to-passage overlap said to persist through the journey because the resilient feet hold down** (draft/08-detailed-description.md, "Registration and retention by the lid", final sentence of the paragraph at line 25) - The disclosure supports only that pressing the resilient feet against the ledges keeps the module from lifting away from the tray during transport, which the immediately preceding sentence of the description already states. It contains no affirmative statement that the horizontal overlap between the peripheral outlet openings and the side supply passages is maintained during transport, and none attributing that maintenance to a downward holding force from the feet. The added sentence asserts a distinct technical result (retention of horizontal registration in transit) and a causal mechanism for it that the source does not describe; a downward clamping force is not the disclosed means of resisting horizontal displacement.
  - Suggested fix: Delete the sentence in its entirety. The preceding sentence ("Closure of the insulated lid 60 compresses the resilient feet 58 between the spacer frame 42 and the ledges 18, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport.") already carries the full supported content, and claims 2, 14 and 18 are unaffected.

Fix every listed item before returning. If an advisory is a false positive, make
the wording or figure specification unambiguous enough that the check passes.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. One tray side wall 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, one of which is seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and the depending indexing rib 62 described below, which enters it from above, are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into the registered position.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, one such ledge 18 and one such resilient foot 58 being seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. Closure of the insulated lid 60 compresses the resilient feet 58 between the spacer frame 42 and the ledges 18, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44. FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, one of which is seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and the depending indexing rib 62 described below, which enters it from above, are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into the registered position.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, one such ledge 18 and one such resilient foot 58 being seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. Closure of the insulated lid 60 compresses the resilient feet 58 between the spacer frame 42 and the ledges 18, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport.
The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44. FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

All three findings are fixed.

- **Condensation mechanism** — the Condensate management paragraph now ends "Condensate present in the guide ducts 50 runs down them and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 into the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods." The clause about moist ambient air condensing on the cassette surfaces and duct walls is gone from the Detailed Description. The Background keeps its own prior-art characterisation, which is where that statement belongs.
- **FIG. 5 tray height** — the brief now gives the thin upright tray wall a lower edge spaced above the top surface of the bottom body immediately inboard of the trough, with the thin horizontal bottom wall joined to that upright wall above its lower edge and the space beneath that bottom wall open, and the vertical space continuing below the wall's lower edge to the bottom body. The tray is no longer drawn sitting at floor level, so FIG. 5 agrees with FIG. 1, FIG. 4, the description and claims 1 and 17 about the lower return passage. The trough, wick and pull tab sentences are unchanged.
- **Transport result** — the sentence attributing persistence of the registered overlap to a downward holding force is deleted. The retention paragraph now ends with the supported statement that closure compresses the resilient feet 58 between the spacer frame 42 and the ledges 18 so the module is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. Claims 2, 14 and 18 are untouched.

input.summary: All three findings are fixed. The Condensate management paragraph now says only that condensate present in the guide ducts runs down them and is delivered through the discharge openings into the condensate channel rather than onto the goods, so the imported account of moist ambient air condensing on the cassettes and duct walls is gone from the Detailed Description while the Background keeps its own prior-art characterisation. The FIG. 5 brief now spaces the thin upright tray wall's lower edge above the top surface of the bottom body, joins the thin horizontal bottom wall to that upright wall above its lower edge with the space beneath it open, and runs the vertical space on down past that lower edge to the bottom body, so the tray is no longer drawn at floor level and FIG. 5 agrees with FIG. 1, FIG. 4, the description and claims 1 and 17. The sentence attributing persistence of the registered overlap to a downward holding force from the resilient feet is deleted, leaving the supported retention statement that closes the paragraph. Numerals across the seven sheets still match the 31 table entries in both directions, every brief is within the length limit with FIG. 4 longest at 2798 characters, and no placeholder or em dash remains.
reasoning: The condensation clause was the clearest kind of defect to cure: invention text borrowing a mechanism from my own Background. Prior-art framing can say where condensate comes from in existing carriers, but the Detailed Description may only say what the inventor said, which is that openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel. The replacement sentence keeps the disclosed route and the disclosed benefit of keeping water off the goods, and drops the origin and the surfaces.

That deletion costs nothing in support. Claims 7 and 16 recite discharge openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharging condensate into the channel, and the paragraph still describes exactly that.

The FIG. 5 contradiction was geometric and would have produced a wrong sheet: joining the tray bottom wall at the lower end of the upright wall while bounding the vertical space down to the floor puts the tray on the floor and erases the lower return passage the perforations open into. Spacing the wall's lower edge above the bottom body, attaching the bottom wall above that edge, and letting the vertical space continue past it restores the tray height that FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 show and that claim 1 requires, without adding any contact or seal.

On the transport sentence, the disclosure supports the module being held down so it cannot lift away, which the preceding sentence already states. Persistence of the horizontal overlap through the journey is a different result, and a downward clamp is not the disclosed means of resisting horizontal movement, so the sentence asserted both an untraced result and an untraced mechanism. Deleting it leaves the retention effect intact and does not touch claims 2, 14 or 18.

No compensating compression was needed: the two description edits shortened their paragraphs, and FIG. 5 grew only to 2677 characters, well inside the limit. No numeral, leader target or curve content moved.

draft/08-detailed-description.md, Registration and retention by the lid: the sentence 'The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.' is deleted.

figures/FIG-5.md: the tray paragraph now gives the thin upright wall a lower edge spaced above the top surface of the horizontal bottom body immediately inboard of the trough, joins the thin horizontal bottom wall to that upright wall above its lower edge and extending leftward with the space beneath it open, and continues the open vertical space below that lower edge to the horizontal bottom body; the trough, wick and pull-tab sentences are unchanged.
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. This turn tightened the boundary between that framing and the invention text by removing a condensation mechanism the Detailed Description had borrowed from it, which strengthens rather than weakens the position: the Background still names the problem, and the description now claims only the disclosed solution. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration, the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. No claim scope moved. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

structured_output.summary: All three findings are fixed. The Condensate management paragraph now says only that condensate present in the guide ducts runs down them and is delivered through the discharge openings into the condensate channel rather than onto the goods, so the imported account of moist ambient air condensing on the cassettes and duct walls is gone from the Detailed Description while the Background keeps its own prior-art characterisation. The FIG. 5 brief now spaces the thin upright tray wall's lower edge above the top surface of the bottom body, joins the thin horizontal bottom wall to that upright wall above its lower edge with the space beneath it open, and runs the vertical space on down past that lower edge to the bottom body, so the tray is no longer drawn at floor level and FIG. 5 agrees with FIG. 1, FIG. 4, the description and claims 1 and 17. The sentence attributing persistence of the registered overlap to a downward holding force from the resilient feet is deleted, leaving the supported retention statement that closes the paragraph. Numerals across the seven sheets still match the 31 table entries in both directions, every brief is within the length limit with FIG. 4 longest at 2798 characters, and no placeholder or em dash remains.
reasoning: The condensation clause was the clearest kind of defect to cure: invention text borrowing a mechanism from my own Background. Prior-art framing can say where condensate comes from in existing carriers, but the Detailed Description may only say what the inventor said, which is that openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel. The replacement sentence keeps the disclosed route and the disclosed benefit of keeping water off the goods, and drops the origin and the surfaces.

That deletion costs nothing in support. Claims 7 and 16 recite discharge openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharging condensate into the channel, and the paragraph still describes exactly that.

The FIG. 5 contradiction was geometric and would have produced a wrong sheet: joining the tray bottom wall at the lower end of the upright wall while bounding the vertical space down to the floor puts the tray on the floor and erases the lower return passage the perforations open into. Spacing the wall's lower edge above the bottom body, attaching the bottom wall above that edge, and letting the vertical space continue past it restores the tray height that FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 show and that claim 1 requires, without adding any contact or seal.

On the transport sentence, the disclosure supports the module being held down so it cannot lift away, which the preceding sentence already states. Persistence of the horizontal overlap through the journey is a different result, and a downward clamp is not the disclosed means of resisting horizontal movement, so the sentence asserted both an untraced result and an untraced mechanism. Deleting it leaves the retention effect intact and does not touch claims 2, 14 or 18.

No compensating compression was needed: the two description edits shortened their paragraphs, and FIG. 5 grew only to 2677 characters, well inside the limit. No numeral, leader target or curve content moved.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. One tray side wall 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, one of which is seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and the depending indexing rib 62 described below, which enters it from above, are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into the registered position.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, one such ledge 18 and one such resilient foot 58 being seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. Closure of the insulated lid 60 compresses the resilient feet 58 between the spacer frame 42 and the ledges 18, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport.
The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Condensate present in the guide ducts 50 runs down them and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 into the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44. FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. One tray side wall 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, one of which is seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and the depending indexing rib 62 described below, which enters it from above, are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into the registered position.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, one such ledge 18 and one such resilient foot 58 being seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. Closure of the insulated lid 60 compresses the resilient feet 58 between the spacer frame 42 and the ledges 18, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport.
The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Condensate present in the guide ducts 50 runs down them and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 into the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44. FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

input.summary: All six findings are fixed. In FIG. 5 the tray side wall now simply carries a thin horizontal bottom wall joined to its lower end with the space beneath open, which removes the undisclosed depending skirt, the lower-edge position and the bypass route, and by the same stroke makes FIG. 5 agree with FIG. 4 and FIG. 1 about where the tray side wall ends. FIG. 1 now states that above the upper edges of the blocks the central space and both channels are continuous across the top of the module body so the stream entering at the centre divides into both channels, which is the disclosed divide-and-descend relationship and matches the open-top frame in FIG. 2. The Detailed Description no longer places the indicator at the outer surface of a side wall, saying only that FIG. 6 shows it as it appears from outside the outer shell 10. A blank line now precedes the circulation path heading, and the FIG. 6 section-designation bullet sits under its own heading. FIG. 1 was tightened elsewhere to hold the new sentence within the length limit and stands at 2790 characters with all bodies, contacts, openings, curve contents and its seven numerals unchanged.
reasoning: The FIG. 5 skirt was the last remnant of a fix I made several rounds ago to stop air bypassing the perforations, and it had become the very thing it was meant to prevent: a lower edge above the floor with the passage carried down past it is a second route out of the side supply passage, and it also fixed which end of a flow boundary was deeper. Joining the bottom wall at the lower end of the upright wall states only the tray the disclosure gives and leaves the perforations as the drawn connection.

That single edit resolves the internal-logic finding too, which is why FIG. 4 and FIG. 1 needed no change. They already showed the tray as a closed open-top box, so bringing FIG. 5 into line with them was the correct direction rather than propagating the skirt outward.

The FIG. 1 continuity gap was the most consequential of the six for the invention: without a statement that the central space and the outboard channels join, the parent view would show hatched material closing the top of each channel and the essential circulation could not be traced on the sheet. The added sentence says only what the disclosed flow requires, that the rising stream divides and passes into the channels, and FIG. 2 already carried the same continuity through its open top.

The indicator location was a small but real overreach in the text. The disclosure says the shell includes an indicator visible from outside and nothing about which wall carries it, so the description now stops at outside the outer shell while FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 keep their schematic side-wall depiction. Claim 9 was already location-neutral and needed no edit.

The two formatting items are worth fixing because both would misread on render: a heading absorbed into a paragraph loses the section structure of the Detailed Description, and a bullet with no heading reads as a detached fragment rather than as the placement instruction for the repeated section designation.

FIG. 1 has sat at its length ceiling for many rounds, so the new sentence was paid for by removing filler in the same brief, an article, a repeated part word and two redundant qualifiers. Nothing structural was traded away and no numeral, leader target or curve content moved.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. This turn strengthens the drawing support for that position, because FIG. 1 now shows the divide-and-descend continuity inside the module that the registered path depends on. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. No claim scope moved. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.
