content.content:
1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Scope: I traced every claim limitation (claims 1-20), every numbered part (10, 12, 14, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54, 56, 58, 60, 62, 64, 70, 72, 74, 76, 80, 82, 84, 86, 100), and every structural, relational, positional, flow-path and operating statement in 04-field through 10-abstract and in figures/FIG-1 through FIG-7 to the disclosure and to the single USER passage in input/conversation.md (which is verbatim identical to input/disclosure.md). The only other conversation turn is labelled YOU (the drafting agent's own report of FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 edits); I treated it as context only, and confirmed the current FIG-1 and FIG-5 briefs do not carry the tray-wall-extension geometry that message described. input/brief.md was used only for title, applicant/inventor, no-priority ("Not applicable" cross-reference) and no-government-support; all three formalities match. Background prior-art characterisations were not traced to the inventor per instruction.
4	
5	Ledger result: the disclosure supports the whole independent-claim structure and every dependent limitation. Specifically supported are the insulated shell/floor/side walls/upper edge, tray on feet with the lower return passage, tray side walls spaced inward forming two side supply passages, perforations, rigid spacer frame with two opposed phase-change cassettes, central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, mating channel, depending indexing rib that shifts the module into the registered position, the fan/pump/powered-air-mover disclaimer, the full circulation path, the compressible gasket sealing after registration, resilient feet pressed on shell ledges, the condensate channel/absorbent wick/pull tab/duct-end discharge openings, and the whole mechanical exposure indicator chain (stem thermally coupled to one cassette, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position, manual reset only after opening, no airflow control), plus the method of claim 17 from the "For use" paragraph. Claim 12 ("rib meets the mating channel while the lid is spaced above the upper edge") and claim 15 ("mating channel opens upward at a top region") are sound inferences from "seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration" and from a depending rib entering the channel from above, so I did not report them. Claim 5 traces to "conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame". The abstract is 141 words and repeats only supported matter. Numeral table, description, briefs and drawing descriptions agree; each numeral means one part; the section line is designated 7-7 identically in the FIG. 6 brief, the FIG. 7 brief and both drawing descriptions; the three broken-line curves in FIG. 1 carry the same FIG. 3 / FIG. 4 / FIG. 5 designations used in the enlarging figures' briefs and drawing descriptions; no drafting note, placeholder, open question, instruction or unresolved alternative remains anywhere; no text says an outline is shown "by way of example" or may have "any closed outline".
6	
7	Three findings, all in the figure briefs, all concerning geometry of functional flow surfaces that the source does not disclose:
8	
9	1. Critical. FIG-1 verbalises a flow topology the inventor never gave: "Above the upper edges of the blocks the central space and both channels are continuous across the top of the body, so the stream entering at the centre divides into both channels." The disclosure routes air only as "enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts"; it never says the two streams cross over the tops of the cassettes, and neither the Detailed Description nor any claim says so. This is a flow-boundary/topology assertion, not an outline convention, and it also sits in tension with the description's "divides along the faces". Delete the sentence.
10	
11	2. Major. FIG-4 verbalises an untapered, constant-section flow boundary: the shell inner surface "is a flat vertical surface running straight from the top of the fragment to the bottom of the fragment". The source says only that "the tray side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages" - nothing about the profile of the surface that bounds that passage. Per the taper/angle rule this is substantive even in a schematic view. Trim to "Its inner surface faces right."; the following sentence already carries the needed statement that the fragment lies below the inward projections.
12	
13	3. Minor. FIG-1 fixes the vertical position of the peripheral outlet port relative to the retention ledge - "opening through the body's outboard side below the projecting block and above the gap". The disclosure gives the outlet openings only as "aligned with the side supply passages" and gives the ledges only as the surfaces the resilient feet press against; their relative height is untraced. Drop the two words "below the projecting block and".
14	
15	I did not report the "shallow ... trough ... wider than it is deep" in FIG-5 (the disclosure says "shallow condensate channel"), the "flat top end surface" gasket seat and "flat upwardly facing top surface" ledge in FIG-3 (minimally generic faces of parts the source affirmatively discloses), or the schematic frame/slab/housing outlines in FIG-2, FIG-6 and FIG-7, each of which is expressly marked "shown schematically" and adds no function or relationship.
16

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical section of an assembled carrier, on a plane cutting both upright blocks in the module body and its top groove. Plain black line work, hatching on cut material, inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined by a thick hatched bottom form a container open at top: the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom the floor 12. Each wall body carries an inward-projecting block below its top. A thick hatched slab across both top ends is the insulated lid 60, closed, a narrow rib projecting down inboard of the left end and a compressible body between slab and each end.

Within it, a sectioned open-top box of thin hatched walls and bottom is the product tray 20, held above the floor 12 by short hatched blocks, two appearing here, shown schematically, the tray feet 22. Its walls stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap each side, with small openings through the tray where each gap meets the space beneath. One shallow trough runs around the tray, cut at both gaps so it appears at each, one elongated absorbent body appearing in both, a narrow strip at one end of the right-hand appearance.

Above the tray, below the lid 60, an elongated hatched body in section is the thermal module 40, open downward at its centre, holding two upright hatched blocks, shown schematically, spaced apart. An open vertical channel runs down outboard of each block, opening through the body's outboard side below the projecting block and above the gap, and at its downward lower end over the trough. Above the upper edges of the blocks the central space and both channels are continuous across the top of the body, so the stream entering at the centre divides into both channels. A small block is flattened between a down-facing outboard surface of the body and each projecting block, the body continuing down inboard. A groove opening upward in the top surface takes the rib's lower end.

All three findings are fixed, all by deletion in the figure briefs.

- **Flow topology over the cassettes** — the sentence placing a continuous region above the upper edges of the blocks, with the incoming stream dividing there, is deleted from `figures/FIG-1.md`. - **Wall profile in FIG. 4** — the first paragraph now reads "Its inner surface faces right." The flat, vertical, full-height run is gone, so the brief no longer asserts a taper-free constant-section passage. The following sentence, which places the fragment below the level of the inward projections, is unchanged and still tells the renderer what it needs.
- **Outlet height relative to the ledge** — "below the projecting block and" is deleted from `figures/FIG-1.md`, so the clause now reads "opening through the body's outboard side above the gap, and at its downward lower end over the trough." The alignment with the side supply passage remains, and no relative height to the retention ledge is stated.

Every deletion shortened its brief, so nothing needed compensating compression. FIG. 1 no longer states that the central space and both channels are continuous above the upper edges of the blocks or that the stream divides there, and no longer places the peripheral outlet opening below the inward-projecting block; the clause now says only that the channel opens through the outboard side above the gap and at its downward lower end over the trough. FIG. 4 no longer gives the shell inner surface a flat, vertical, full-height profile, saying only that it faces right, with the sentence placing the fragment below the inward projections left intact. Nothing was added anywhere and no application text changed. Every deletion shortened its brief, numeral coverage still matches the table exactly in both directions, all seven briefs are within the length limit, and no placeholder or em dash remains.
reasoning: The continuity sentence was mine, added last round to cure a different finding, and it overshot. The disclosure routes air along the faces of the cassettes and down the guide ducts; saying the central space and both channels run together above the cassette tops states where the split happens and what bounds it, which is flow topology rather than outline. It also disagreed with the description, which says the rising stream divides along the faces, and with the same brief's own top surface carrying the groove.

Deleting it does not leave the sheet unable to show the path. The module body is still open downward at its centre, each channel still runs down outboard of a block and opens through the outboard side above the gap and at its lower end over the trough, and FIG. 4 still shows the outlet feeding the side supply passage. The renderer has the disclosed geometry without the brief settling a question the inventor left open.

The wall profile was gratuitous as well as untraced: no other brief describes that same wall by anything but which way its surfaces face, and the sentence that follows already tells the renderer the fragment sits below the ledges. A flat vertical full-height run asserts a constant-section, taper-free passage, which the source never gives.

The outlet height was the smallest of the three but the same class of statement. The disclosure ties the outlet openings to the side supply passages and ties the ledges to the resilient feet, and never relates the two, so fixing the port below the ledge asserts where the module discharges relative to its hold-down interface. Keeping above the gap preserves the disclosed alignment.

All three were deletions, so no compensating compression was needed and no numeral, leader target or curve content moved. I made no replacement text and touched no file in draft/, since the description and claims were already correct and adding to them to justify a drawing would invert the authority order.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn only deleted untraced geometry from two figure briefs, so no claim scope moved and the claims still rest on the disclosed division along the cassette faces and descent through the guide ducts. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

# FIG. 2

Perspective view of the thermal module alone, seen from above and in front so the open top, the near long side wall and the right short end wall are visible. Plain black line work on white, no hatching, all inside the drawing area.

The main body is a rectangular open frame, shown schematically, with near and far long side walls, left and right short end walls and a bottom panel joining them, its top open. This frame is the spacer frame 42; with the two slabs it holds it is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, parallel to the long side walls, their extent along the frame shown schematically. They are spaced apart across the frame depth, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each is spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between slab and wall. The slab nearer the front is the first phase-change cassette 44, the slab nearer the back the second phase-change cassette 46, each a plain closed box, shown schematically.

In the bottom panel, within the open central gap between the slabs, a rectangular through opening is drawn, so the viewer looks down through the panel there. This opening is the central inlet opening 48.

A further through opening passes down through the bottom panel at the foot of the channel beside each slab, so the viewer looks down through the panel there and each channel is open at its lower end.

Along the lower part of the near long side wall, at the foot of the channel beside the first phase-change cassette 44, a rectangular opening passes through the wall. This is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54. A matching opening in the far long side wall is concealed behind the second phase-change cassette 46.

The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove, shown schematically. This groove is the mating channel 56.

The lower part of each long side wall carries an outward step, shown schematically, having a downwardly facing surface outboard of the frame. Small blocks project down from that surface, two visible at the front, shown schematically. These blocks are the resilient feet 58.

- 54: on the opening in the near long side wall.
- 56: well inside the groove in the top edge of the near long side wall.

1. A passive cold-chain carrier comprising:

an insulated outer shell having a floor, side walls and an upper edge;

a product tray removably received in the outer shell, the product tray having a bottom wall, tray side walls, perforations, and tray feet standing on the floor so that the product tray is supported above the floor and a lower return passage remains between the bottom wall and the floor, the tray side walls being spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell so that two side supply passages are formed;

a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, the thermal module comprising a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings positioned to align with the side supply passages, and a mating channel; and

an insulated lid closable on the upper edge of the outer shell and carrying a depending indexing rib positioned to enter the mating channel as the insulated lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages;

the carrier being free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the outer shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the insulated lid cooperating in the registered position to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations, and returns through the lower return passage.

2. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the spacer frame carries resilient feet, the outer shell has ledges beneath the resilient feet, and closure of the insulated lid presses the resilient feet against the ledges so that the thermal module is held down against lifting away from the product tray.

3. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a compressible lid gasket carried by the insulated lid and arranged to seal against the upper edge of the outer shell after the depending indexing rib has shifted the thermal module into the registered position.

4. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the two opposed phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame with an inner face of a first phase-change cassette confronting an inner face of a second phase-change cassette across a central space, and the central inlet opening opens downward into the central space.

5. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame.

6. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a shallow condensate channel extending around the product tray, and a removable absorbent wick lying in the condensate channel.

7. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 6, wherein the spacer frame further defines discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, the discharge openings discharging condensate into the condensate channel.

8. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 6, wherein the absorbent wick carries a pull tab that remains accessible when the product tray is removed from the outer shell, so that the absorbent wick is replaceable without opening a phase-change cassette.

9. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a mechanical exposure indicator carried by the outer shell and visible from outside the carrier, the mechanical exposure indicator comprising an indicator stem thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes, a temperature-responsive latch retaining the indicator stem in a stowed position, and a spring biasing the indicator stem toward an exposed position, the temperature-responsive latch releasing the indicator stem when said one of the phase-change cassettes softens.

10. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 9, wherein the exposed position is a latched position in which the mechanical exposure indicator retains the indicator stem after said one of the phase-change cassettes has cooled again, the mechanical exposure indicator being resettable manually only after the carrier is opened.

11. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 9, wherein the mechanical exposure indicator does not control airflow, the circulation path being the same whether or not the indicator stem stands in the exposed position.

12. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the depending indexing rib meets the mating channel while the insulated lid is spaced above the upper edge of the outer shell, and remaining closing travel of the insulated lid translates the spacer frame horizontally into the registered position.

13. A thermal module for a passive cold-chain carrier having an insulated outer shell, a product tray defining side supply passages with side walls of the outer shell, and an insulated lid carrying a depending indexing rib, the thermal module comprising:

a rigid spacer frame sized to be removably received in the outer shell above the product tray; and

two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame;

the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening through which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the spacer frame, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes and receiving air that has divided along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings positioned to align with the side supply passages, and a mating channel positioned to be entered by the depending indexing rib as the insulated lid closes so that the thermal module is shifted into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

15. The thermal module of claim 13, wherein the mating channel opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame.

16. The thermal module of claim 13, wherein the spacer frame further defines discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts and positioned to discharge condensate into a condensate channel extending around the product tray within the outer shell.

17. A method of transporting temperature-sensitive goods, the method comprising:

fitting two conditioned phase-change cassettes to a rigid spacer frame of a thermal module, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings, and a mating channel;

placing the goods in a product tray and placing the product tray in an insulated outer shell so that tray feet of the product tray stand on a floor of the outer shell, leaving a lower return passage between the product tray and the floor and two side supply passages between tray side walls of the product tray and side walls of the outer shell;

placing the thermal module in the outer shell above the product tray;

closing an insulated lid on an upper edge of the outer shell so that a depending indexing rib carried by the insulated lid enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages; and

thereafter transporting the goods while air circulates, without operation of any powered air mover, along a circulation path in which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage.

18. The method of claim 17, wherein closing the insulated lid further presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, retaining the thermal module against lifting away from the product tray during the transporting, and compresses a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell after the thermal module has been shifted into the registered position.

19. The method of claim 17, further comprising, after the transporting, opening the insulated lid, removing the product tray from the outer shell, and drawing a removable absorbent wick, by a pull tab of the absorbent wick, out of a condensate channel extending around the product tray within the outer shell, without opening a phase-change cassette.

input.summary: Both findings are fixed. The FIG. 2 outward step is now placed above the peripheral outlet opening 54 rather than on the lower part of each long side wall, so it no longer occupies the same height band as that port and no longer contradicts FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, which put the resilient feet and shell ledges in the upper region next to the closed lid while the outlet belongs to the lower FIG. 4 region. Claim 14 now recites that the thermal module is held down against lifting away from the product tray, matching claim 2, claim 18, the Detailed Description and the disclosure. Numeral coverage still matches the table exactly in both directions, all seven briefs are within the length limit with FIG. 2 longest at 2787 characters, and the numeral table, Brief Description, Detailed Description and other briefs were not touched.
reasoning: The FIG. 2 conflict was a real cross-view contradiction about one part. FIG. 1 encloses the feet and ledges in the upper left curve that FIG. 3 enlarges, and puts the outboard channel opening in the lower left curve that FIG. 4 enlarges, so the feet sit well above the outlet. Saying the step is above the peripheral outlet opening ties the two features together by a relationship the other sheets already establish, rather than by a new height that no source gives, and it keeps the step from being drawn across the port it would otherwise obstruct.

I anchored the step to the outlet opening rather than to the frame's top or bottom because that is the relationship the drawing set already fixes, and because the disclosure relates the feet only to the shell ledges and the outlets only to the side supply passages. An absolute height would have been a new assertion; a relative order that FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 already imply is not.

Claim 14 said the module is held down against the product tray, which reads as the module bearing on the tray. The disclosure says only that it cannot lift away from the tray, and claim 2, claim 18 and the description all use that formulation. Conforming claim 14 removes a relationship the source never states and makes one element read the same way across the whole claim set. It narrows nothing, since bearing on the tray was never the disclosed retention effect.
Nothing else moved. The step edit lengthened FIG. 2 only slightly and it remains inside the limit, no numeral or leader target changed, and the claim edit touched a single clause.

reasoning: The FIG. 2 conflict was a real cross-view contradiction about one part. FIG. 1 encloses the feet and ledges in the upper left curve that FIG. 3 enlarges, and puts the outboard channel opening in the lower left curve that FIG. 4 enlarges, so the feet sit well above the outlet. Saying the step is above the peripheral outlet opening ties the two features together by a relationship the other sheets already establish, rather than by a new height that no source gives, and it keeps the step from being drawn across the port it would otherwise obstruct.

I anchored the step to the outlet opening rather than to the frame's top or bottom because that is the relationship the drawing set already fixes, and because the disclosure relates the feet only to the shell ledges and the outlets only to the side supply passages. An absolute height would have been a new assertion; a relative order that FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 already imply is not.

The disclosure says only that it cannot lift away from the tray, and claim 2, claim 18 and the description all use that formulation. Conforming claim 14 removes a relationship the source never states and makes one element read the same way across the whole claim set. It narrows nothing, since bearing on the tray was never the disclosed retention effect.

Perspective view of the thermal module alone, seen from above and in front so the open top, the near long side wall and the right short end wall are visible. Plain black line work on white, no hatching, all inside the drawing area.

The main body is a rectangular open frame, shown schematically, with near and far long side walls, left and right short end walls and a bottom panel joining them, its top open. This frame is the spacer frame 42; with the two slabs it holds it is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, parallel to the long side walls, their extent along the frame shown schematically. They are spaced apart across the frame depth, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each is spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between slab and wall. The slab nearer the front is the first phase-change cassette 44, the slab nearer the back the second phase-change cassette 46, each a plain closed box, shown schematically.

In the bottom panel, within the open central gap between the slabs, a rectangular through opening is drawn, so the viewer looks down through the panel there. This opening is the central inlet opening 48.

A further through opening passes down through the bottom panel at the foot of the channel beside each slab, so the viewer looks down through the panel there and each channel is open at its lower end.

Along the lower part of the near long side wall, at the foot of the channel beside the first phase-change cassette 44, a rectangular opening passes through the wall. This is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54. A matching opening in the far long side wall is concealed behind the second phase-change cassette 46.

The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove, shown schematically. This groove is the mating channel 56.

Each long side wall carries an outward step, shown schematically, above the peripheral outlet opening 54, the step having a downwardly facing surface outboard of the frame. Small blocks project down from that surface, two visible at the front, shown schematically. These blocks are the resilient feet 58.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 40: outside the frame outline, with a lead line and arrow to the module as a whole.
- 42: on the right short end wall, well inside its outline.
- 44: well inside the visible upper face of the front slab.
- 46: well inside the visible upper face of the rear slab.
- 48: well inside the opening in the bottom panel between the slabs.
- 54: on the opening in the near long side wall.
- 56: well inside the groove in the top edge of the near long side wall.
- 58: well inside one of the small blocks projecting below the step at the front.

content.text:
The finding is fixed in the two figure briefs.

- `figures/FIG-2.md` — the step paragraph now reads "Each long side wall carries an outward step, shown schematically, the step having a downwardly facing surface outboard of the frame." The elevation relationship to the peripheral outlet opening 54 is gone. The step, its downwardly facing outboard surface, the schematic blocks and numeral 58 all remain, since the disclosure affirmatively gives resilient feet of the spacer frame pressed against ledges of the shell.
- `figures/FIG-4.md` — "The fragment is taken below the level of the inward projections of the wall bodies." is replaced by "The inward projections of the wall bodies lie outside this fragment." That still tells the renderer no ledge appears in this view, stated positively as a view-scope fact, without asserting a direction relative to the outlet port.

Both edits shortened their briefs, so nothing needed compensating compression. No file in `draft/` changed: the claims, the Detailed Description, the Brief Description and the numeral table never recited this relationship, and claim 2 still says only that the outer shell has ledges beneath the resilient feet. Numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions, all seven briefs are within the length limit with FIG. 2 longest at 2747 characters, and no placeholder or em dash remains.

input.summary: The finding is fixed in the two figure briefs. FIG. 2 no longer places the resilient-foot step above the peripheral outlet opening 54, reading now that each long side wall carries an outward step, shown schematically, having a downwardly facing surface outboard of the frame. FIG. 4 no longer says its fragment is taken below the level of the inward projections; it now states positively that the inward projections of the wall bodies lie outside this fragment, which still tells the renderer no ledge appears in the view without asserting a direction relative to the outlet port. The step, its outboard bearing surface, the schematic blocks, numeral 58 and the schematic ledge elsewhere all remain, because the disclosure gives resilient feet of the spacer frame pressed against ledges of the shell. No file in draft/ changed, both edits shortened their briefs, numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions, and all seven briefs are within the length limit with FIG. 2 longest at 2747 characters.
reasoning: The elevation statement was mine from the previous round, added to separate the step from the outlet port after a cross-view conflict, and it solved that conflict by asserting something the inventor never said. The disclosure ties the feet to the ledges and the outlets to the side supply passages and never relates the two, so fixing one above the other decides whether the ledge stands in the path the port discharges into. That is flow-boundary substance, not an outline choice, and the schematic tag does not reach it.

Removing it does not reopen the earlier conflict, because the sheets no longer make competing claims about that height at all: FIG. 2 simply gives the frame an outward step with a downwardly facing outboard surface, and FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 continue to show a foot flattened between such a surface and a ledge top, which is the disclosed relationship.

For FIG. 4 I used a positive view-scope sentence rather than the earlier directional one. Saying the projections lie outside this fragment gives the renderer the same practical instruction, that no ledge is drawn here, while stating a fact about the view instead of a fact about the invention, and it avoids the negative linework phrasing that failed an earlier gate.

I changed nothing in draft/. Claim 2 recites only that the outer shell has ledges beneath the resilient feet, and neither the description nor the Brief Description recites any relationship to the outlets, so the text was already correct and adding to it to justify a drawing would invert the authority order.
Both edits are deletions or substitutions that shortened their files, so no compensating compression was needed and no numeral, leader target or curve content moved.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn removed one untraced elevation relationship from two figure briefs, so no claim scope moved. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

# FIG. 5

Enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1 enclosed by the broken-line curve there designated FIG. 5, seen horizontally in section on the right side of the carrier. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the right portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part and extends leftward.

In the upper left part of the drawing area, a hatched portion of the module body is drawn in section. An open vertical channel passes down through this module body, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel, an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the module body. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.

Below the module body, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the left of the inner surface of the upright wall body, and a thin hatched horizontal bottom wall joined to the lower end of that upright wall and extending leftward, the space beneath that bottom wall being open. A series of small openings passes through the product tray where that upright wall meets that bottom wall, as in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. An open vertical space runs down between the upright wall body and the thin wall to the horizontal bottom body, so that the downward opening in the module body stands above that space.

In the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body, at the foot of the open vertical space and below the discharge opening 76, a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, wider than it is deep. This trough is the condensate channel 70.

An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip, shown schematically, extends from one end of the absorbent body, its free end clear of the absorbent body. This strip is the pull tab 74.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the module body.
- 70: inside the trough, clear of the absorbent body.
- 72: well inside the elongated absorbent body lying in the trough.
- 74: well inside the narrow strip extending from the absorbent body.
- 76: on the opening through the bottom surface of the module body.

The geometry paragraph now ends with the open vertical space running down between the shell wall body and the thin tray wall so that the downward opening in the module body stands above that space, and no longer calls the tray perforations the only connection between that space and the space beneath the tray bottom wall. Everything else in the brief is untouched, including the tray wall joined to the tray bottom wall with the space beneath open, the small openings through the product tray where they meet, the trough outboard of the thin upright wall and below the discharge opening 76, the wick, the pull tab and the numeral list. reasoning: The exclusivity clause was mine, added last round to keep the passage from bypassing the perforations, and it went wrong in two ways at once. The disclosure recites the air's route through the perforations but never says that is the only route, and the tray is expressly suspended above the floor on feet, so the region beneath it is open. Saying the perforations are the sole connection asserts a flow boundary the inventor did not give, and a schematic label cannot carry that kind of statement.

It was also unachievable from the geometry in the same brief: with the tray wall ending at the tray bottom wall, the space beneath that wall open, and the trough in the floor outboard of the tray wall, the two spaces necessarily meet below the tray wall's lower edge. A brief that specifies geometry and then denies its consequence cannot be rendered faithfully either way.

Deleting the clause is enough because the disclosed route is still drawn. The small openings through the product tray where the upright wall meets the bottom wall remain in FIG. 5, FIG. 4 still says the side supply passage opens through them into the space beneath the bottom wall, and FIG. 1 still shows small openings where each gap meets the space beneath. The claims recite the path in order without exclusivity, so text and drawings now say the same thing.
I left FIG. 1, FIG. 4 and every file in draft/ untouched. They were already correct, and editing them to accommodate a figure statement would invert the authority order.
The edit was subtractive, so nothing needed compensating compression and no numeral, leader target or curve content moved.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn deleted one untraced clause from a figure brief, so no claim scope moved and the claimed circulation path is unchanged. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

content.text:
All three findings are fixed, all inside the figure briefs.

- **Outward step and stepped frame profile** — `figures/FIG-2.md` now reads "Each long side wall carries a downwardly facing surface at its outboard side, shown schematically." The step as a named structure is gone, while the feet still project down from that outboard surface, which is what the disclosed pressing of the resilient feet against the shell ledges requires. In `figures/FIG-1.md` the trailing clause about the body continuing down inboard is deleted, so the sentence now reads "A small block is flattened between a down-facing outboard surface of the body and each projecting block." FIG. 3 and the Detailed Description were already traced and are untouched.
- **Trough proportion** — `figures/FIG-5.md` now reads "a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, shown schematically", dropping the width-to-depth relationship. The trough's position in the top surface of the bottom body, outboard of the tray wall and below the discharge opening 76, is kept, as is "shallow", which is the inventor's own word.
- **Orphan label list** — `figures/FIG-6.md` now has the heading "Other labels shown on this figure" above the section-designation bullet, with the doubled blank line collapsed. The bullet text and the numerals section below it are unchanged.

Numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions, all seven briefs are within the length limit with FIG. 2 longest at 2713 characters, and no placeholder or em dash remains. No file in `draft/` changed.

input.summary: All three findings are fixed inside the figure briefs. FIG. 2 no longer adds an outward step to the spacer frame, saying only that each long side wall carries a downwardly facing surface at its outboard side, shown schematically, with the resilient feet projecting down from that surface. FIG. 1 no longer states that the module body continues down inboard of the foot, so the sentence now ends with the small block flattened between a down-facing outboard surface of the body and each projecting block. FIG. 5 drops the width-to-depth proportion for the condensate trough, which is now a shallow upwardly open trough drawn in section, shown schematically, keeping its position outboard of the tray wall and below the discharge opening 76. FIG. 6 now carries the heading Other labels shown on this figure above the section-designation bullet, with the doubled blank line collapsed. No file in draft/ changed, numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions, all seven briefs are within the length limit with FIG. 2 longest at 2713 characters, and no placeholder or em dash remains.
reasoning: The outward step was a structural feature I had added to the spacer frame across two briefs, and it decided how the retention joint is built. The disclosure says only that the closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell, which leaves open whether the feet depend from a step, from a plain outboard face, or from a boss. Reducing FIG. 2 to a downwardly facing outboard surface keeps the one relationship the source gives, a surface from which the feet press down onto the ledge, and stops the drawing from settling the rest.

The FIG. 1 clause about the body continuing down inboard was the matching profile statement, so it had to go with the step. Its removal costs nothing the sheet needs: the small block is still flattened between the body's down-facing outboard surface and the projecting block, which is the contact FIG. 3 and the Detailed Description already describe.

FIG. 3 and the description were left alone deliberately. They state the flattened foot between a downwardly facing outboard surface of the frame and the upwardly facing ledge top, which the reviewer traced as supported, and editing them to match a figure would have inverted the authority order.

The trough proportion was an unhedged dimensional statement about a functional collection feature. The inventor gives only the word shallow, which the brief still uses; wider than it is deep added a ratio the source never supplied and, unlike the wick and tab in the same paragraph, carried no schematic tag. Replacing it with the schematic marker keeps the trough drawable without asserting its section.

The FIG. 6 heading is a formatting fix, but a real one: an orphan bullet after a blank gap reads as a stray fragment rather than a label-placement instruction, and every other brief introduces its bullets with a heading. I used a heading distinct from the numerals heading because a section designation is annotation, not a reference numeral, and it must stay out of the numeral list and numerals.md.
All four edits shortened or left level their files, so nothing needed compensating compression and no numeral, leader target or curve content moved.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn removed untraced frame structure and one dimensional statement from the figure briefs and fixed a heading, so no claim scope moved; claims 2, 14 and 18 still recite the resilient feet pressed against the ledges without reciting how the frame carries them. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged view of the upper side region of FIG. 1 enclosed by the broken-line curve there designated FIG. 3, seen horizontally in section with the lid closed. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

A thick hatched upright wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from an upper end down to the lower edge of the fragment, its outer surface facing left and its inner surface facing right. This is one of the side walls 14 of the sectioned outer shell. Partway down the inner surface, a hatched block projects rightward from it with a flat upwardly facing top surface, shown schematically. This projection is one of the ledges 18.

Across the upper part of the drawing area lies a thick hatched horizontal closure slab, shown in section, spanning rightward past the middle of the drawing area, its underside facing the top end of the upright wall body.

A small hatched body of compressible material lies between the underside of the closure slab and the flat top end surface of the upright wall body, contacting both and flattened between them. This body is the compressible lid gasket 64.

Inboard of the compressible lid gasket 64, a narrow rib projects downward from the underside of the closure slab, extending below the level of the top end of the upright wall body. This projection is the depending indexing rib 62.

To the right of the upright wall body, spaced from its inner surface, a hatched body is drawn in section extending from beneath the closure slab downward past the lower edge of the fragment, so that it is shown cut off there. This body is the sectioned spacer frame 42. Its upper edge carries an upwardly open groove that receives the lower end of the depending indexing rib 62. This groove is the mating channel 56.

At the level of the ledge 18, a small block lies between a downwardly facing outboard surface of the sectioned spacer frame 42 and the upwardly facing top surface of the ledge 18, contacting both and flattened between them. This block is one of the resilient feet 58.

- 42: well inside the sectioned frame body, clear of the groove.

- 58: well inside the block resting on the top surface of the ledge.

The disclosure gives the existence of the ledge and the fact that the gasket seals against the upper edge, and says nothing about either profile, so neither word could stand as a depiction convention.

I kept upwardly facing on the ledge because it is entailed: the feet are pressed down onto the ledge, so the surface they meet must face up. That is a direction the disclosed action forces, not a profile the drawing chose.

The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn deleted two words from one figure brief, so no claim scope moved; claims 2, 3, 14 and 18 still recite the feet pressed against the ledges and the gasket sealing after registration without reciting any face profile. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

# FIG. 2

Perspective view of the thermal module alone, seen from above and in front so the open top, the near long side wall and the right short end wall are visible. Plain black line work on white, no hatching, all inside the drawing area.

The main body is a rectangular open frame, shown schematically, with near and far long side walls, left and right short end walls and a bottom panel joining them, its top open. This frame is the spacer frame 42; with the two slabs it holds it is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, parallel to the long side walls, their extent along the frame shown schematically. They are spaced apart across the frame depth, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each is spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between slab and wall. The slab nearer the front is the first phase-change cassette 44, the slab nearer the back the second phase-change cassette 46, each a plain closed box, shown schematically.

In the bottom panel, within the open central gap between the slabs, a rectangular through opening is drawn, so the viewer looks down through the panel there. This opening is the central inlet opening 48.

A further through opening passes down through the bottom panel at the foot of the channel beside each slab, so the viewer looks down through the panel there and each channel is open at its lower end.

Along the lower part of the near long side wall, at the foot of the channel beside the first phase-change cassette 44, a rectangular opening passes through the wall. This is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54. A matching opening in the far long side wall is concealed behind the second phase-change cassette 46.

The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove, shown schematically. This groove is the mating channel 56.

Each long side wall carries a downwardly facing surface at its outboard side, shown schematically. Small blocks project down from that surface, two visible at the front, shown schematically. These blocks are the resilient feet 58.

The finding is fixed, and one related defect that had reappeared is now cured durably.

- **FIG. 2 numeral note for 58** — the entry now reads "- 58: well inside one of the small blocks projecting down from the downwardly facing outboard surface at the front." The word "step" is gone, so the leader targets the feature the body of the same brief actually describes and no stepped side-wall profile is implied for the spacer frame. Nothing else in FIG. 2 changed.
- **FIG. 6 orphan bullet** — the section-designation bullet had lost its heading again and was sitting after a doubled blank line. I removed the bullet and the extra blank line rather than re-adding a heading that keeps being stripped. Nothing is lost: the cutting-plane paragraph already states in prose that the upper end carries a short arrow pointing toward the left of the drawing area with the section designation 7 beside it, that the lower end carries a second arrow pointing the same way with the designation 7 repeated, and that the repeated designation makes the line read line 7-7. FIG. 7 and both Brief Description entries still read "line 7-7 of FIG. 6".

Numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions, FIG. 6 keeps its four numerals, all seven briefs are within the length limit with FIG. 2 longest at 2747 characters, and no placeholder or em dash remains. No file in `draft/` changed.

The FIG. 2 leader entry for numeral 58 now reads that it sits well inside one of the small blocks projecting down from the downwardly facing outboard surface at the front, so it targets the feature the body of that brief describes and imports no stepped profile onto the spacer frame. In FIG. 6 the section-designation bullet had again lost its heading and was sitting after a doubled blank line, so I deleted the bullet and the extra blank line instead of re-adding a heading that keeps being stripped; nothing is lost, because the cutting-plane paragraph already states in prose that each end carries an arrow pointing toward the left of the drawing area with the section designation 7 beside it and repeated, giving line 7-7, and FIG. 7 and both Brief Description entries still read line 7-7 of FIG. 6. Numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions, FIG. 6 keeps its four numerals, all seven briefs are within the length limit with FIG. 2 longest at 2747 characters, and no file in draft/ changed.
reasoning: The 58 entry was left behind when I removed the outward step from the FIG. 2 body last round. A leader instruction that points at a feature the brief no longer defines is unrenderable, and the word step would have put a shoulder back on the spacer frame that the disclosure never gives. Aligning the entry to the downwardly facing outboard surface fixes both problems with no change to the invention.

I also dealt with the FIG. 6 bullet, because it is the same defect a reviewer raised two rounds ago and my earlier fix did not hold: the heading I added was stripped again, leaving the bullet orphaned. Adding the heading a third time would have failed the same way, so I removed the bullet instead.

That removal is safe because the bullet was redundant. The prose paragraph already specifies both arrows, their common direction, the designation 7 beside each, and that the repeated designation makes the line read line 7-7, which is exactly what the section-line check requires of a source-view brief. The designation also stays out of the numeral list and numerals.md, where a section designation does not belong.

Nothing in draft/ needed touching. The Brief Description and FIG. 7 already name line 7-7 of FIG. 6, the numeral table has no entry for a section designation, and the claims and description say nothing about a step.
Both edits are wording-level and subtractive, so no compensating compression was needed and no numeral, leader target or curve content moved.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn corrected one leader instruction and removed one redundant bullet, so no claim scope moved. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

A passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed in which the closing of the lid, rather than the care of the packer, establishes the circulation path.

In one aspect, the carrier includes an insulated outer shell having a floor and side walls, a product tray removably received in the outer shell, a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, and an insulated lid. The product tray is supported above the floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains between the product tray and the floor, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell to form two side supply passages. The thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib positioned to enter a mating channel of the spacer frame as the lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

In the registered position the shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the lid cooperate to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover.

The technical effect of lid-driven registration is that the alignment on which the circulation path depends is created by an act the packer cannot omit. The thermal module is placed in the outer shell above the product tray, and the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel shifts the module into the position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The seal made by a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell occurs after registration, so the carrier is not closed against a module that is still out of position. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it during transport.

In a further aspect, a shallow condensate channel extends around the product tray and receives a removable absorbent wick. Discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts deliver condensate into the condensate channel. A pull tab on the absorbent wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, so the wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service.

In a further aspect, the outer shell carries a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside the carrier. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position, and the indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again, being reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator therefore reports the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends, survives recovery of the cassette, and requires no battery. The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.

In a further aspect, a method includes fitting conditioned phase-change cassettes to the spacer frame, placing product in the product tray, placing the product tray in the outer shell, placing the thermal module above the product tray, and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into the registered position, whereafter air circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover.

The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. One tray side wall 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, one of which is seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and the depending indexing rib 62 described below, which enters it from above, are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into the registered position.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, one such ledge 18 and one such resilient foot 58 being seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. Closure of the insulated lid 60 compresses the resilient feet 58 between the spacer frame 42 and the ledges 18, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Condensate present in the guide ducts 50 runs down them and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 into the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44. FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

reasoning: Both sentences were inherited boilerplate, and boilerplate is exactly where an unsupported broadening slips in unnoticed. The inventor drew the line explicitly: the registered passive circulation path around the removable tray and opposed cassettes, combined with lid-driven registration, is the essential relationship, and only the wick and the irreversible indicator are optional. A blanket may be used together or separately contradicts that partition and offers an embodiment set the disclosure does not contain.

The Detailed Description version was worse because it contradicted the paragraph directly above it in the same section, which lists the optional parts by numeral. A document that names its essential features and then invites their omission two lines later is internally inconsistent, and that inconsistency is the kind a later reader would use against the specification.

The replacements keep the useful work boilerplate does. The Summary still disclaims itself as a statement of claim scope, and the description still says the implementations are examples and may otherwise be varied within the scope of the claims, so nothing is narrowed that the disclosure supports; only the specific invitation to drop the essentials is gone.

I made no change to the claims. Claim 1 and claim 17 recite the registered path and the lid-driven registration as required elements and the optional features appear only in dependent claims, so the claim set already reflected the inventor's partition correctly.
Nothing in the figure briefs was involved, and both edits are single-sentence replacements, so no numeral, leader target or curve content moved.
